source_text: Διὰ ταῦτα καὶ Παῦλος εἰργάζετο διηνεκῶς, οὐκ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ μόνῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ νυκτί· καὶ τοῦτο βοᾷ λέγων· Νυκτὸς γὰρ καὶ ἡμέρας ἐργαζόμενοι, πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαί τινα ὑμῶν. Καὶ οὐχ ἁπλῶς τέρψεως ἕνεκεν καὶ ψυχαγωγίας τὸ ἔργον μετῄει, καθάπερ πολλοὶ τῶν ἀδελφῶν, ἀλλὰ τοσοῦτον ἐπεδείκνυτο περὶ αὐτὸ πόνον, ὡς καὶ ἑτέροις δυνηθῆναι ἐπικουρῆσαι. Ταῖς γὰρ χρείαις μου, φησὶ, καὶ τοῖς οὖσι μετ' ἐμοῦ ὑπηρέτησαν αἱ χεῖρες αὗται. Ἄνθρωπος δαίμοσιν ἐπιτάττων, τῆς οἰκουμένης διδάσκαλος ὢν, τοὺς τὴν γῆν οἰκοῦντας ἅπαντας ἐπιτραπεὶς, καὶ τὰς ὑφ' ἡλίῳ κειμένας Ἐκκλησίας ἁπάσας, καὶ δήμους καὶ ἔθνη καὶ πόλεις μετὰ πολλῆς θεραπεύων ἐπιμελείας, νύκτα καὶ ἡμέραν εἰργάζετο, καὶ οὐδὲ μικρὸν ἀνέπνει τῶν πόνων ἐκείνων. Ἡμεῖς δὲ, οὐδὲ τὸ μυριοστὸν τῆς ἐκείνου φροντίδος μετιόντες, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐδὲ εἰς νοῦν λαβεῖν δυνάμενοι, διατελοῦμεν ἐν ἀργίᾳ ζῶντες διηνεκῶς. Καὶ ποίαν ἕξομεν ἀπολογίαν, ἢ τίνα συγγνώμην, εἰπέ μοι; Ἐντεῦθεν ἅπαντα εἰς τὸν βίον εἰσενήνεκται τὰ κακὰ, ὅτι πολλοὶ μεγίστην ἀξίαν εἶναι νομίζουσι, τὸ μὴ τὰς ἑαυτῶν μεταχειρίζειν τέχνας, καὶ ἐσχάτην κατηγορίαν, τὸ φανῆναί τι τοιοῦτον εἰδότας. Καὶ Παῦλος μὲν οὐκ ᾐσχύνετο ὁμοῦ καὶ σμίλην μεταχειρίζων, καὶ δέρματα ῥάπτων, καὶ τοῖς ἐν ἀξιώμασι διαλεγόμενος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐνεκαλλωπίζετο τῷ πράγματι, μυρίων πρὸς αὐτὸν λαμπρῶν καὶ ἐπισήμων ἀφικνουμένων ἀνθρώπων. Καὶ οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνετο ταῦτα ποιῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ καθάπερ ἐν στήλῃ χαλκῇ ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ἐξεπόμπευσεν ἑαυτοῦ τὸ ἐπιτήδευμα. Ὅπερ οὖν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἔμαθε, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα αὐτὸ μετεχείριζε, καὶ τότε μετὰ τὸ εἰς οὐρανὸν τρίτον ἁρπαγῆναι, μετὰ τὸ εἰς παράδεισον ἀπενεχθῆναι, μετὰ τὸ κοινωνῆσαι ῥημάτων ἀποῤ ῥήτων τῷ Θεῷ· ἡμεῖς δὲ, οὐδὲ τῶν ὑποδημάτων ὄντες ἄξιοι τῶν ἐκείνου, αἰσχυνόμεθα τούτοις, ἐφ' οἷς ἐκεῖνος ἐνηβρύνετο· καὶ καθ' ἑκάστην μὲν ἡμέραν πλημμελοῦντες, οὐδὲ ἐπιστρεφόμεθα, οὐδὲ ὄνειδος εἶναι νομίζομεν· τὸ δὲ ἐκ δικαίων πόνων ζῇν, ὡς αἰσχρὸν καὶ καταγέλαστον φεύγομεν. Τίνα οὖν ἕξομεν ἐλπίδα σωτηρίας, εἰπέ μοι; Τὸν γὰρ αἰσχυνόμενον, ἁμαρτίαν αἰσχύνεσθαι δεῖ, καὶ τὸ τῷ Θεῷ προσκροῦσαι, καὶ τὸ ποιῆσαί τι τῶν οὐ δεόντων, ἐπὶ δὲ τέχναις καὶ ἐργασίαις καὶ ἐναβρύνεσθαι. Οὕτω γὰρ καὶ πονηρὰν ἔννοιαν τῇ τῆς ἐργασίας ἀσχολίᾳ τῆς διανοίας ἐκβαλοῦμεν ῥᾳδίως, καὶ τοῖς δεομένοις ἐπικουρήσομεν, καὶ τὰς ἑτέρων οὐκ ἐνοχλήσομεν θύρας, καὶ τὸν νόμον τοῦ Χριστοῦ πληρώσομεν τὸν εἰπόντα· Μακάριόν ἐστι διδόναι μᾶλλον ἢ λαμβάνειν. Διὰ γὰρ τοῦτο χεῖρας ἔχομεν, ἵνα ἑαυτοῖς βοηθῶμεν, καὶ τοῖς τὰ σώματα πεπηρωμένοις ἐκ τῶν ἡμετέρων εἰσφέρωμεν τὰ κατὰ δύναμιν ἅπαντα· ὡς ἐάν τις ἀργῶν διατελῇ, κἂν ὑγιαίνῃ, τῶν πυρεττόντων ἐστὶν ἀθλιώτερος· οἱ μὲν γὰρ παρὰ τῆς ἀσθενείας ἔχουσι συγγνώμην, καὶ τύχοιεν ἂν ἐλέου· οὗτοι δὲ καταισχύνοντες τὴν τοῦ σώματος εὐεξίαν, εἰκότως ἂν παρὰ πάντων μισοῦνται, ὡς καὶ τοὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ παραβαίνοντες νόμους, καὶ τῇ τραπέζῃ τῶν ἀσθενούντων λυμαινόμενοι, καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἑαυτῶν φαυλοτέραν ποιοῦντες. Οὐδὲ γὰρ τοῦτο μόνον ἐστὶ τὸ δεινὸν, ὅτι δέον οἴκοθεν καὶ παρ' ἑαυτῶν τρέφεσθαι, τὰς ἑτέρων ἐνοχλοῦσιν οἰκίας, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ πάντων αὐτοὶ γίνονται χείρους.
thought_title: Paul's manual labor as a boast, and the shame of idleness
orientation: Chrysostom is addressing his congregation, contrasting Paul's tireless tentmaking with their own idleness and misplaced shame about manual work.
pass_a_gloss: For these reasons Paul also worked continually, not only in the day, but also in the very night; and he shouts this, saying: For working night and day, so as not to burden any of you. And not simply for the sake of pleasure and diversion did he pursue the work, as many of the brothers do, but he displayed so much toil in it, as to be able also to help others. For my needs, he says, and those who are with me, these hands served. A man commanding demons, being teacher of the inhabited world, entrusted with all those dwelling on the earth, and caring for all the churches under the sun, and peoples and nations and cities with much care, worked night and day, and did not even briefly catch breath from those labors. But we, not undertaking even the ten-thousandth part of his concern, or rather not even able to bring it to mind, continue living in idleness continually. And what defense will we have, or what pardon, tell me? From this all evils have been brought into life, that many consider it a very great dignity not to practice their own trades, and a final accusation to appear knowing any such thing. And Paul was not ashamed, at the same time handling the knife and sewing hides and conversing with those in dignities, but he even prided himself on the matter, while countless splendid and distinguished men came to him. And not only was he not ashamed doing these things, but also, as on a bronze pillar, in his letters he publicly displayed his own occupation. What therefore he learned from the beginning, he also practiced after these things, and then after being snatched up to the third heaven, after being carried away to paradise, after sharing in unutterable words with God; but we, not being worthy even of the sandals of that man, are ashamed of these things, in which that man exulted; and while sinning every day, we do not even turn back, nor do we consider it a reproach; but living from righteous labors, as something shameful and ridiculous, we flee. What hope of salvation then will we have, tell me? For the one who is ashamed, ought to be ashamed of sin, and of offending God, and of doing any of the things not proper, but in trades and work also to exult. For thus we shall easily cast out also the wicked thought by the occupation of the mind with work, and we shall help those in need, and we shall not trouble the doors of others, and we shall fulfill the law of Christ who said: It is blessed to give rather than to receive. For this reason we have hands, in order that we may help ourselves, and may bring in to those maimed in body from our own resources all things according to our power; so that if anyone continues idle, even if he is healthy, he is more wretched than those with fever; for those have pardon from weakness, and would obtain mercy; but these, disgracing the good condition of the body, would reasonably be hated by all, as both transgressing the laws of God, and harming the table of the weak, and making their own soul more worthless. For this alone is not the terrible thing, that when they ought to be nourished from home and from themselves, they trouble the houses of others, but that they themselves become worse than all.

choices.why: The smilē is a cutting tool used by leatherworkers; 'knife' keeps the manual-labor concreteness without over-specifying.
The verb means to take pride or glory in something; 'prided himself' captures the reflexive boasting force.
Ekpompeuō means to parade or exhibit publicly; 'publicly displayed' fits the bronze-pillar image.
Enabrynomai means to take pride or exult in; 'exulted' conveys the positive boastful delight.

pass_b_english: For this reason Paul also worked constantly—not only by day, but even in the night itself. And he proclaims it, saying, “Working night and day, so as not to burden any of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:9). Nor did he pursue the work merely for pleasure and recreation, as many of the brothers do. Instead, he showed such toil in it that he was able to help others as well. “These hands,” he says, “served my needs and those who were with me” (Acts 20:34). A man who commanded demons, who was the teacher of the world, who had been entrusted with all the inhabitants of the earth, who cared with great diligence for all the churches under the sun, and for peoples and nations and cities—this man worked night and day, and did not catch even a small breath from those labors. But we, who do not undertake even a ten-thousandth part of his care—rather, we cannot even bring it to mind—we live in idleness continually. And what defense will we have, or what pardon, tell me? From this all evils have entered life: that many consider it the greatest dignity not to practice their own trades, and the worst accusation to appear knowing any such thing. Paul was not ashamed to handle an awl and sew hides at the same time as he conversed with people of rank. No—he prided himself on the matter, even while countless brilliant and distinguished people came to him. And not only was he not ashamed to do these things, but he publicly displayed his occupation in his letters as if on a bronze pillar. What he had learned from the beginning, he continued to practice afterward as well—even after being snatched up to the third heaven, after being carried away to paradise, after sharing unutterable words with God. But we, who are not worthy even of his sandals, are ashamed of the very things in which he exulted. Every day we sin, and we do not turn back, nor do we consider it a disgrace. But living from honest labors we flee as something shameful and ridiculous. What hope of salvation will we have, then, tell me? For the one who is ashamed should be ashamed of sin, and of offending God, and of doing anything improper—but in trades and work he should exult. For in this way we will easily cast out wicked thoughts through the occupation of the mind with work, and we will help those in need, and we will not trouble the doors of others, and we will fulfill the law of Christ, who said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). For this reason we have hands: so that we may help ourselves, and so that we may contribute from our own resources everything in our power to those whose bodies are maimed. So if anyone continues in idleness, even if he is healthy, he is more wretched than those with fevers. For the sick have pardon from their weakness, and they may obtain mercy. But the idle, disgracing the good condition of their body, are rightly hated by all, since they both transgress the laws of God, and plunder the table of the weak, and make their own soul more worthless. For this is not the only terrible thing—that when they ought to feed themselves from their own home and resources, they trouble the houses of others—but also that they themselves become worse than everyone.

problems.source_quote: Νυκτὸς γὰρ καὶ ἡμέρας ἐργαζόμενοι, πρὸς τὸ μὴ ἐπιβαρῆσαί τινα ὑμῶν
problems.why: The quote matches 2 Thessalonians 3:8 or 1 Thessalonians 2:9, but the source has plural 'ἐργαζόμενοι' (we working), not Paul's singular. Chrysostom attributes this to Paul speaking of himself and his companions. The citation 1 Thess 2:9 uses singular 'ἐργαζόμενος' in NA28; the plural form here matches 2 Thess 3:8. The verse reference is incorrect for the quoted form.
problems.ruling: Source has plural ἐργαζόμενοι matching 2 Thess 3:8, not 1 Thess 2:9's singular ἐργαζόμενος.

fixed: Changed the scripture citation from 1 Thessalonians 2:9 to 2 Thessalonians 3:8 because the quoted Greek has the plural participle 'ἐργαζόμενοι' (working), which matches 2 Thessalonians 3:8, not the singular form in 1 Thessalonians 2:9.

problems.fix: "Working night and day, so as not to burden any of you" (1 Thessalonians 2:9)

last_rejected.ruling: πεπηρωμένοις is perfect passive participle of πηρόω, meaning 'maimed, disabled, crippled'; 'maimed' is within normal semantic range.

last_rejected.quote: and did not catch even a small breath from those labors
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ οὐδὲ μικρὸν ἀνέπνει τῶν πόνων ἐκείνων
last_rejected.why: ἀνέπνει means 'breathe' not 'catch breath'; 'did not breathe' or 'had no respite' is the sense—he didn't get even a small breathing-space/rest from those labors.
last_rejected.fix: and had not even a small respite from those labors
last_rejected.ruling: ἀνέπνει means 'breathe'; 'catch breath' is a natural English idiom for respite. No meaning lost.

last_rejected.why: ἐσχάτην here means 'utmost, extreme' not 'worst'; 'the highest/extreme reproach/condemnation' is meant—it's about social disgrace, not a legal accusation.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐσχάτην κατηγορίαν: 'worst accusation' is within normal range; 'extreme' and 'worst' overlap adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἀξιώμασι means 'dignities, high offices, positions of honor'—'people in high office' or 'people of high position,' not general 'rank.'
last_rejected.ruling: τοῖς ἐν ἀξιώμασι: 'people of rank' is a standard rendering for those holding dignities/positions.

last_rejected.why: λαμπρῶν means 'splendid, illustrious, distinguished' in social status; 'brilliant' suggests intellectual brightness, which is misleading.
last_rejected.ruling: λαμπρῶν: 'brilliant' commonly means 'illustrious, distinguished' for persons; not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: he publicly displayed his occupation in his letters as if on a bronze pillar
last_rejected.source_quote: καθάπερ ἐν στήλῃ χαλκῇ ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ἐξεπόμπευσεν ἑαυτοῦ τὸ ἐπιτήδευμα
last_rejected.why: ἐξεπόμπευσεν means 'paraded, made a show of' with pride; 'publicly displayed' is too neutral. The verb is stronger—he 'paraded' or 'showed off' his trade.
last_rejected.fix: he paraded his occupation in his letters as on a bronze pillar
last_rejected.ruling: ἐξεπόμπευσεν: 'publicly displayed' captures the verb's sense adequately; 'paraded' is a preference.

last_rejected.quote: and plunder the table of the weak
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ τῇ τραπέζῃ τῶν ἀσθενούντων λυμαινόμενοι
last_rejected.why: λυμαινόμενοι means 'ravaging, doing harm to, damaging'—'plunder' is too strong (suggests theft); 'ravage' or 'burden' or 'drain' is closer.
last_rejected.fix: and burden the table of the weak
last_rejected.ruling: λυμαινόμενοι: 'plunder' is within the word's range of 'damage, ruin, prey upon'; not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: they themselves become worse than everyone
last_rejected.why: Missing object: χείρους is comparative 'worse' but the Greek says 'they themselves become worse than all'—worse than all other people, not just 'everyone' vaguely.
last_rejected.fix: they themselves become worse than all
last_rejected.ruling: πάντων χείρους: 'worse than everyone' correctly renders the comparative; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: But living from honest labors we flee as something shameful and ridiculous
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ἐκ δικαίων πόνων ζῇν, ὡς αἰσχρὸν καὶ καταγέλαστον φεύγομεν
last_rejected.why: The subject 'we' is clear but the Greek has τὸ...ζῇν (the infinitive 'to live'), making it 'but to live from honest labors we flee'—the English 'living' as participle loses the articular infinitive construction which emphasizes 'the act of living by honest labors.' Minor but the nominal sense is stronger in Greek.
last_rejected.fix: But to live from honest labors we flee as something shameful and laughable
last_rejected.ruling: τὸ ζῇν as articular infinitive: 'living' captures the sense; nominal emphasis is stylistic, not a meaning change.
